About Classical Watch

About Classical Watch

I'm George Mount, founder of Stringfest Analytics. Part of the inspiration for the name Stringfest comes from string instruments and classical music.

I love classical music, and when I can't get to a live concert, putting on a livestream is one of my favorite ways to relax. It's great music, but also wonderful ambiance while I'm working or spending time around the house.

Here in Cleveland, we're fortunate to have an amazing classical music and conservatory scene. There are also so many great conservatories around the country and the world, and many offer free concerts and livestreams. I wanted a simple place to discover those performances, focused specifically on free conservatory livestreams. That's why I built Classical Watch.

A small experiment, built with AI

I built Classical Watch with help from Codex. It brings together two things I enjoy: classical music and turning scattered information into something useful. It's a little project I use myself, and I hope you enjoy it too.

This is an independent calendar of free streams from conservatories and university music schools. Concerts open on the school's own viewing service. Questions, corrections, or a livestream we missed? Contact George.

Before you tune in

Times are shown in your time zone. The calendar is updated daily and looks up to 45 days ahead, as schools announce their streams. Schedules can change, so check the linked event page before watching. Some streams, including certain Juilliard performances, need a free account.

Today's concerts stay visible until midnight in your time zone, so you can still open the stream if a performance runs late. “Started earlier” means the scheduled end has passed; the school controls whether the stream is still available.

Saved calendar events don't update automatically. If a school hasn't supplied an end time, we reserve 90 minutes as an estimate.

Browse the schools

Music enrollment uses published music-school figures, not the size of the whole university. Figures are approximate and may come from different years; where a comparable figure isn't available, it is marked “Not listed.”

    How to watch on your TV

    George's preferred setup: Chrome on a laptop

    I usually open the concert in Chrome on my laptop and cast it to the TV. In my experience, this often works better than trying to cast my phone screen.

    1. Connect your laptop and a TV with Google Cast—or a Chromecast or Google TV Streamer—to the same Wi-Fi network.
    2. Open Classical Watch in an up-to-date Chrome browser, choose a concert, and select Watch stream. Start the video on the school's page.
    3. Open Chrome's three-dot menu, choose Cast, save and share, then Cast…. Choose your TV. If a Sources menu appears, select Cast tab so the concert audio goes to the TV too.
    4. Make the video full-screen and keep your laptop awake. To finish, select Chrome's Cast icon and Stop casting.

    If the player has its own Cast button, you can use that directly. No compatible TV or casting device? An HDMI cable from your laptop to the TV is another simple option.

    Google's casting guide includes troubleshooting and the permission needed on newer Macs.
